name: Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's New Residence
aka: the new residence Beaubien built at the homestead
one of the buildings on lots 6-10 of Block 5

documented_range.note: THE BUILDING IS ATTESTED AND ITS DATES ARE NOT, SO BOTH BOUNDS ARE HOUSEKEEPING BOUNDS AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. Andreas, scan p. 185, lists what the Beaubien homestead held; `docs/RESEARCH/jb_beaubien_homestead.md` § 1 reads it as the American Fur Company factory building, a new residence, a small trading post and a cabin converted to a barn. The list gives no year to any of the three that are not the factory building. THE OPENING BOUND IS THE SAME FLOOR THE PARENT RECORD USES AND FOR THE SAME REASON: Andreas has Beaubien in the Dean house at the lake shore from 1817 'for several years' and at the factory building from 1822 (scan pp. 191, 205), and Wentworth finds the residence at this corner 'after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house', so 1822-01-01 is the earliest date the sources leave open and not a construction date. THE CLOSING BOUND IS THE END OF THE SCENE YEAR, not a demolition date: what carries the survival is Wentworth's own account of the sale of June 1839, where James H. Collins bids $1,049 for lots 10, 9, 8, 7 and 6 'where Beaubien's house, out-buildings, and garden were' — four years after 1835-07-01, and evidence that the group was still standing, not that this building was one of the things named. THE 13-YEAR SPAN WILL RAISE THIS PROJECT'S WIDE-RANGE WARNING and is left standing rather than trimmed to silence it, exactly as both siblings do: the warning is correct that nothing documents the middle years.

placement.position_note:
PLACED BY EYE INSIDE A GROUP, WHICH IS THE HONEST DESCRIPTION OF IT, and it is the same method and the same admission `beaubien_barn` carries. NOTHING LOCATES THIS BUILDING. Andreas records it in a list of what the homestead held and gives it no bearing, no distance and no neighbour. METHOD: the group's two committed records stand on one easting 16.3 m apart — `jb_beaubien_homestead` on the frontage line and `beaubien_barn` on the yard line behind it — and this record takes an easting 17.9 m east of that pair, which puts it 5.7 m clear of the house's east wall on the SAME line as the building of the group it belongs beside. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE BOTH INVENTED. East was chosen rather than west because Wentworth's own lot list runs the homestead ground north from the corner along lots 6 to 10, so the group's room is away from the corner and not back across the avenue, and because the fort's stockade stands 9 m north of this line and there is no room that way.

THE CAVEAT THAT TRAVELS WITH THE PARENT, UNCHANGED: neither South Water Street nor Michigan Avenue existed on the reservation in 1835 — it was unplatted and no street crossed it — so the corner both books locate this group by is a grid that arrived with the 1839 plat. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus the parent's own unmeasured northward offset (lots 6-10 lie north of corner lot 11, so the group's true position is at the corner or north of it), plus an unquantified allowance for placing an undescribed building beside a building located by a retrospective address. Facade bearing 0, north toward the river, inherited from the parent record and attested nowhere.
placement.symbolic_location: On the Fort Dearborn reservation, in the Beaubien homestead group at what Andreas and Wentworth call the north-east corner of South Water Street and Michigan Avenue — modelled on the frontage line beside the factory building, about 6 m east of it.

footprint.note: INVENTED. No source gives this building a dimension. 9.75 x 6.1 m is 32 x 20 ft: the 20 ft depth is borrowed from Hogan's store, the one log footprint in this dataset with a documented dimension and the figure the parent record borrows too, and 32 ft is between the parent's 40 ft frontage and the barn's 20 ft — a two-pen log house with a chimney, larger than the cabin Beaubien moved out of and smaller than the trade house he moved into. Every number is invented and this polygon cites no sources. IT IS DRAWN AS A HOUSE AND NOT AS A MANSION: Andreas's word is 'residence' and Wentworth's is 'traditional residence', and neither carries a size.

construction.note: NOT STATED BY ANY SOURCE REACHED, and it is the same reading `jb_beaubien_homestead` and `beaubien_barn` both carry: log, from date and place. Nothing reached dates this building, so the earliest it can have gone up is 1822 and the latest is the scene date; this project's dossier records the settlement's stock as log until frame arrived with the town, and excludes brick on the south side before 1837. If it was in fact frame this record has the right massing on the wrong archetype and should move to a frame archetype rather than being repainted.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill — the same reading and the same number this project gives Hogan's store, `beaubien_barn` and this record's parent.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region, and it is what both committed buildings of this group carry.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is this archetype's mid-range for a low single-storey log building roofed in riven shakes, and is the figure the other two buildings of this group carry. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

stories.note: INVENTED. No source gives this building a storey. One is the smaller claim and the archetype's default, and it is what both committed buildings of this group carry; a prosperous trader's 'new residence' could as easily have been a storey and a half, and guessing upward would make the group read grander than anything reached says it was.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One is the minimum for a building lived in through Chicago winters and the archetype's default. The COUNT is the inference; the stack's position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

function.note: 'He afterwards built a new residence and a small trading post' — Andreas, scan p. 185, in the sentence that lists what the homestead held. THE USE IS DOCUMENTED IN FOUR WORDS AND NOTHING ELSE ABOUT THE BUILDING IS. Note what is NOT claimed here: the parent record's own `occupants` block says that WHICH building of the group Beaubien slept in on the scene date is unattested, and this record does not answer that by being called a residence — it carries no occupants at all, and the household stays where the evidence left it.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS 85 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

research_note: THE SECOND OF THE FOUR BUILDINGS ANDREAS RECORDS AT THIS HOMESTEAD, AND THE ONE WITH THE MOST ROOM IN IT. WHY THIS IS BUILT NOW, WHEN THE DOSSIER SAID IT WOULD NOT BE. `docs/RESEARCH/jb_beaubien_homestead.md` § 4 read 'the homestead was four buildings and one is modelled' and refused the other three on the ground that they 'would be three invented boxes placed by eye around a fourth'. That sentence is now two releases out of date on its own count — `beaubien_barn` was built on 2026-08-11 in exactly the way § 4 forbids, by eye, 16.3 m behind the house, with the direction and the distance recorded as invented — so the refusal had already been overturned for one of the three and was still written down for all three. T-1712 takes the owner's own ask for this ground (T-1203, 'the documented country seats with their reconstructed neighbours') and applies the barn's disposition to the two buildings left: the PRESENCE is attested, the POSITION and the SIZE are invented and graded `reconstructed`, and § 4 is rewritten to the count it now has. WHAT IS NOT DONE: nothing is upgraded on any committed record, the household is not moved onto either new building, and the garden the 1839 sale names with the out-buildings is still unbuilt — it is ground cover and a fence line, not a structure, and no source gives it an extent. REVIEW IS FLAGGED on this record for the reason both of its siblings carry it: the Fort Dearborn reservation, the Beaubien family's place in the Indian trade at Chicago and the Potawatomi removal of August 1835 all meet on this ground, and AGENTS.md's standing constraint asks for consultation rather than for a reconstruction that settles the question by building something. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD: the 1839 land-sale plat of Block 5 with the lot dimensions Wentworth's numbers imply, which would turn 'lots 6 to 10' into a distance north of the corner and fix the whole group to lots rather than to a remembered intersection; failing that, the Wright 1834 sheet read at reservation scale, or the 1835 pre-emption papers, which may describe the improvements Beaubien was claiming for.
